items.title: Muse Spark Open
items.content:
Muse Spark Open is available today and brings leading agentic capabilities to your desktop for the first time on Apple M5 Ultra Mac Studios.

Today, we’re releasing the weights for Muse Spark Open, the most capable US open-weight model to date. Muse Spark Open is a natively multimodal model with 816B total parameters (42B active) and a 1M-token context window. Built for coding and agentic work, it excels at long-horizon tasks, complex software engineering, and multi-step reasoning.

We believe the future is for everyone , and that includes the freedom to run advanced models wherever, including at home. Muse Spark Open is the first model in its class to run on your desktop using two Apple M5 Ultra Mac Studios with the latest MLX framework.

Muse Spark Open is available today through API platforms at Baseten, Fireworks AI, Groq, Modal, Nebius, OpenRouter and Together AI. Model weights are available for download on Amazon SageMaker AI, Google Cloud Model Garden, Hugging Face, and Microsoft Foundry Models.

It runs on leading inference engines like SGLang, vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, Hugging Face Transformers, Apple MLX, llama.cpp, and Unsloth with optimizations for AMD, Apple, Intel, and NVIDIA silicon. Developers can easily further customize the model using the PyTorch framework.

For more details about our evaluations, see the evaluation methodology report .

Leveraging the latest version of MLX, Muse Spark Open was optimized to run on Mac Studio with M5 Ultra, and together they’re the best way to run a powerful model on your own desktop.

Apple’s unified memory architecture lets the M5 Ultra's integrated GPU use up to 512 GB per Mac Studio, so two machines can hold an entire model. And the chip’s 1.2 TB/s of memory bandwidth is fast enough to read the small slice each token needs. The result is two Mac Studios behave like one supercomputer with a terabyte of unified memory.

We tested a range of agentic workflows running entirely on-device, using Muse Code powered by Muse Spark Open, including shipping real iOS changes to Ice Cubes (an open-source Mastodon client) — bug fixes, new features, full build — and driving DaVinci Resolve end to end, with the model reviewing footage frame by frame to find the strongest moments and crop them vertically.

We’re sharing this work because we want everyone to have access to the best models. The open-weight version of Muse Spark ships with custom, auto-tunable Helion GPU kernels in SGLang, delivering 1.03-3.95× kernel-level speedups on NVIDIA and AMD GPUs, and a 3% end-to-end speedup on AMD MI350.

Releasing open-weight models is part of how we bring the benefits of personal superintelligence to everyone, and part of how safety work advances across the field.

Open weights also carry their own considerations , and Muse Spark Open has additional safety post-training for that reason. The results demonstrate strong safeguards across risk categories measured.

We evaluated the model in line with our Meta Superintelligence Scaling Framework , covering the most severe risks, and it met the thresholds our framework requires for release. Detailed results are in the Muse Spark Open model card , with a full evaluation report available soon.

We’re releasing the weights under the Muse Model License with limited commercial terms, which allow many developers to use the model for free.

You can customize Muse Spark Open for your use case by leveraging PyTorch’s TorchTitan to further tune the model. To run it on Apple silicon, use MLX, which pulls the weights directly from Hugging Face.

Muse Spark Open is available now through Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/collections/meta-models/muse-spark-open

MLX Adapter for running Muse Spark Open on Mac Studio.

Hosted Inference Partners: Together AI, Fireworks, Baseten, Modal, Groq, Nebius, and OpenRouter.

Built or published something with Muse Spark Open? Share with us on the Hugging Face Forums — we’d love to see what you create.

You are seeing this because the administrator of this website has set up Anubis to protect the server against the scourge of AI companies aggressively scraping websites. This can and does cause downtime for the websites, which makes their resources inaccessible for everyone.

Anubis is a compromise. Anubis uses a Proof-of-Work scheme in the vein of Hashcash, a proposed proof-of-work scheme for reducing email spam. The idea is that at individual scales the additional load is ignorable, but at mass scraper levels it adds up and makes scraping much more expensive.

Ultimately, this is a placeholder solution so that more time can be spent on fingerprinting and identifying headless browsers (EG: via how they do font rendering) so that the challenge proof of work page doesn't need to be presented to users that are much more likely to be legitimate.

Please note that Anubis requires the use of modern JavaScript features that plugins like JShelter will disable. Please disable JShelter or other such plugins for this domain.

Linux creator and longtime lead maintainer Linus Torvalds turned to Anthropic’s Claude Code to tackle a kernel performance problem that developers have struggled with for more than two years. On Tuesday, he submitted a 10-patch series that delivered a 23-fold throughput improvement in a synthetic benchmark running on his Ryzen Threadripper.

Torvalds had spent 18 months running a broken version of his own fix for the page-cache reference-counting bottleneck, while other developers had encountered problems with their approaches. The new patches eliminate folio reference-count operations from a common buffered-read path, although Torvalds warned that the benchmark gains would be considerably smaller in real-world workloads.

Reviewers have since identified a race condition and raised concerns about memory reclamation. Torvalds has handed further development to Kiryl Shutsemau , a Linux kernel developer who previously worked on the same bottleneck.

On Torvalds’ Core i7-8565U laptop, folio reference-count contention accounted for 99.92% of cross-core load HITMs in eight-thread tests, according to Hardware Busters .

The bottleneck was flagged in 2024 by Matthew Wilcox, an Oracle engineer and longtime Linux kernel memory-management developer, after it surfaced in a customer workload.

On Sunday, Phoronix’s Michael Larabel spotted an experimental branch named noref-filemap-read-with-llm in Torvalds’ tree, which rarely contains anything outside the main development branch.

The eight-patch series, based on Linux 7.3-rc6, came with a clear account of what Claude Code did. Torvalds said the assistant wrote the implementation, tests, and initial documentation, and reviewed the code under his direction. He ran the benchmarks himself, despite having previously criticized developers for claiming AI writes 99% of their code .

Earlier approaches copied data without holding a folio reference and checked its validity afterward, leaving races involving reclamation and replacement. The subsequent 10-patch rcu-free-v3 series instead uses a new PG_rcu_free flag and RCU-delayed reclamation to protect the folio through the userspace copy, provided it doesn’t fault.

items.title: Voting Rights and Privacy Organizations Sue Trump-Vance Administration Over Secretive Collection of Millions of Americans’ Voter Records
items.content:
Lawsuit Challenges DHS’s Unlawful Effort to Build a Nationwide Voter Database Containing Sensitive Personal Information from at Least 47 States

Washington, D.C. — The League of Women Voters, the Electronic Privacy Information Center (EPIC), and the League of United Latin American Citizens (LULAC) filed a lawsuit today challenging the Trump-Vance administration’s secretive and unlawful effort to collect and compile sensitive personal information about millions of American voters into a massive nationwide database. The plaintiffs are represented by Democracy Forward and Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW).

The lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, challenges the U.S. Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) collection, maintenance, and use of voter registration records from at least 47 states as part of a sweeping effort to investigate unsubstantiated claims of voter fraud. The plaintiffs allege that DHS has exceeded its legal authority, violated federal privacy protections, and put the personal information and rights of millions of Americans at risk.

According to the complaint, DHS has obtained and processed voter records containing highly sensitive personal information, potentially including Social Security numbers, driver’s license numbers, dates of birth, home addresses, voting histories, and political affiliations. The agency has also combined voter records with information purchased from commercial data brokers, creating an even more extensive collection of Americans’ personal information.

The lawsuit alleges that DHS has undertaken this sweeping surveillance effort without legal authority or the transparency required by federal law, and without giving the public an opportunity to understand or challenge how it collects and uses personal information.

Internal government records and other disclosures cited in the complaint reveal the unprecedented scope of the administration’s efforts:

The complaint also highlights the administration’s repeated reliance on inaccurate claims of widespread noncitizen voting. In one instance , DHS publicly claimed to have identified nearly 16,000 noncitizens registered to vote in Nevada. After further examination, DHS reduced that number to 185, and Nevada officials determined that every one of those individuals was a U.S. citizen.

“DHS is sweeping up our most sensitive data by any means necessary to fuel its anti-immigration agenda and chase down nonexistent voter fraud. As part of this agenda, the agency is greatly overstepping its authority, violating federal privacy law, and trampling on our privacy, fundamental rights, and democratic values,” said Alan Butler, Executive Director and President of EPIC . “EPIC is proud to join the League and LULAC to stand up against this blatant abuse of our data and defend the fundamental right to privacy.”

“The federal government has no business secretly collecting the sensitive personal information of millions of American voters and feeding it into immigration enforcement systems under the guise of election security,” said  Celina Stewart, CEO of the League of Women Voters . “Let’s be clear: Voting is a fundamental right, not a privilege granted by this administration, and our personal information is not theirs to exploit. The League will not stand by while this administration weaponizes voter data, undermines public trust, and threatens our fundamental freedoms.”

“Linking voter rolls to immigration enforcement is voter intimidation, and LULAC will not stand for it. We have seen these tactics before. For nearly a century, those in power have tried to scare Latinos away from the ballot box with purges, threats, and false claims of fraud, and every time we have fought back and won. This administration claims it is going after undocumented people on the voter rolls, but that lie is being used to purge eligible voters from every community, including women. items.title: Neural networks are clean
items.content:
The cause of polysemanticity in early model organisms wasn’t superposition, but several ordinary, mostly fixable issues. We can now understand most neurons in models up to trillions of parameters, and think the outlook for mechanistic interpretability may be far better than we thought.

A working hypothesis · 65-minute read · Text version

I think I have good news about the nature of neural networks.

After many months studying neurons and circuits in image and language models, I’ve come to believe a network’s own mechanisms are its legible building blocks, and that the outlook for mechanistic interpretability may be far better than I’d feared. The canonical evidence of polysemanticity and superposition that convinced much of the field, including me, that networks pack concepts arbitrarily was misread. What looked like arbitrary packing was mostly a motif I’ll call recursive generalization, which is much less concerning. This means we can study networks directly, instead of first untangling them. Neural networks are already clean.

There are at least two ways to approach mechanistic interpretability. The first is rapid normal science on the network itself: look at a network’s neurons and circuits, study how they relate, watch data flow through them, and run experiments at agentic scale to test explanations. The second starts from a list of hypothesized features and tries to extract them all, designing increasingly sophisticated reconstruction objectives and usually ignoring the original.

The field began with the first approach and fell back to the second because neural networks seemed to be tangled knots. We had canonical examples of polysemantic neurons, the broad name for a neuron that appears to have multiple unrelated jobs or that looks impossible to understand. The most famous one, in an image model, responded to both cat faces and the fronts of cars. And the last layer of the early field’s model organism, InceptionV1, seemed so full of arbitrary mixtures it wasn’t clear how to study it: almost none of the neurons were easily interpretable.

The leading explanation for polysemanticity was superposition. This proposed a new learning principle: when a neural network runs out of neurons, it stops grouping related things together and instead begins folding unrelated things together, simply because they don’t interfere. The result is a kind of knot: the network could have folded in many almost equally good ways, so which things a neuron groups together tells you almost nothing. You have to unfold the knot before you can study anything. In practice that means training a second model – a decomposition such as a sparse autoencoder – to approximate the network as it would look unfolded and studying that instead. If the network really is knotted, there may be no alternative.

One main result is that superposition was the wrong explanation for InceptionV1. Architectural problems made later layers overflow. Weak interpretability tools amplified these problems, making the late layers seem incoherent. Since then, architectural changes designed to help deep layers learn better have had the unintended effect of making them more interpretable. When we first studied InceptionV1, we found almost no interpretable neurons in its last layer. But with these ordinary improvements, and no change to model size or training data, 99-100% of neurons in that last layer are easily interpretable and the model is broadly legible the whole way through. It’s the first non-trivial neural network I feel I mostly understand; you can browse it here . I trained versions of it across a 300× range in size, and it’s broadly legible at every scale. With less room, the network doesn’t fold unrelated things together; its neurons just cover coarser-grained concepts, like one car neuron covering many kinds of car. With more room, that neuron differentiates into many specific cars. So the problem wasn’t the presence of a second learning principle, it was just an…

items.title: JPEG XL vs AVIF for web use-cases
items.summary: compsci, web
items.content:
JPEG XL has now landed in all major browsers, so I figured I'd take a closer look at what it's good/bad at compared to other formats.

I'll go into full detail, with examples and benchmarks, but for those of you who don't have the time, here are the headlines:

For lossy photos on the web, AVIF almost always produces smaller files than JPEG XL. At default effort settings, the best JPEG XL version is typically 15–25% larger than the equivalent AVIF. At maximum effort settings, the gap narrows a little, to typically 6–20%. There are outliers, where JPEG XL is close to, or even beats AVIF, so if you want the absolute best result for a particular image, it's worth trying both. See the F1 image for a typical example, and the weasel for an outlier.

The JPEG XL encoder matters a lot. jixel , a newer JPEG XL encoder, usually produces smaller files than libjxl , except when the image has detailed transparency. The people image is one example.

For screenshots and illustrations, AVIF is much better than JPEG XL. The equivalent JPEG XL is 30–90% larger at default effort settings, and 20–70% larger at maximum effort settings. Lossy AVIF handles these well - you don't need to use lossless formats unless you really need bit-exact results. See the screenshot and illustration examples.

For images with transparency, AVIF is much better than JPEG XL. The libjxl version is 31–44% larger at default effort settings, and 61–70% larger at maximum effort settings. jixel always encodes transparency losslessly, which makes its files 2–3x the size of AVIF's. See the data .

AVIF is generally faster to encode, and uses less memory, when you factor in file size. jixel is faster than AVIF and uses less memory, but its files are typically significantly larger, so AVIF is better on balance. See the F1 image for one example.

AVIF is faster to decode. JPEG XL typically takes 2–3x as long to decode at medium quality, but the gap narrows at very high qualities, where Chrome can sometimes decode JPEG XL faster. The people image is one example.

Higher effort settings are worth it for AVIF and jixel, but not libjxl. libjxl's higher efforts are much slower, use a lot more memory, and barely improve the result. Sometimes they produce larger files than the default effort. The screenshot is an example of this.

AVIF's 4:2:0 mode (half colour resolution) shouldn't be your default. It rarely reduces file size, and it makes higher qualities harder to reach. Although, it is quicker to encode and decode. Stick with 4:4:4 if you don't have time to check both. The F1 image is one example, and the screenshot is an exception.

Quality settings are reliable for all the encoders. With a single quality setting, the resulting quality varies a bit between images, but all the encoders vary in the same direction, and in ways that seem reasonable. See the data .

Progressive JPEG XL is basically free at high effort. jixel recently added support for early progressive previews, and at its slowest setting they cost little or nothing, but at its default setting the files are 12% bigger. Firefox and Chrome support progressive JPEG XL. Safari still renders the final image, but doesn't show progressive previews. However, is this type of progressive rendering a good user experience? See the examples and data .

AVIF supports progressive rendering! It's Chrome-only for now, but it's in progress for Firefox. It's more complex than progressive JPEG XL, but it gives you more control over what the preview looks like, the files are usually smaller, and they're much faster to decode. See for yourself .

For HDR, JPEG XL lacks gain maps, which is a significant limitation compared to AVIF. The JPEG XL format supports gain maps, but they aren't supported by browser decoders, and the encoding story is messy/experimental. When comparing non-gain mapped HDR content, the two quality metrics I used disagree a lot, but they agree that JPEG XL produces smaller files compared to AVIF. See the examples…

items.title: Incident Report: unsanctioned agent behaviour during cyber testing | AISI Work
items.content:
You can access the full technical report here.

AISI’s role is to evaluate and understand the capabilities of frontier AI models, surfacing potential risks before they reach the public. To assess what these models can do, including whether they could be misused for cyberattacks, we test them under deliberately permissive conditions: with access to the open internet, and with some safety filters disabled.

On 28 th July 2026, AISI's Security Team detected unusual data transfers leaving our research systems during a routine cyber evaluation. On investigation, we found that some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations. We declared a security incident and, within roughly one hour of discovery, had contained it and begun a full investigation.

The incident stemmed from a single evaluation where agents were given a task of solving a cyber security challenge. We ran this challenge 122 times across several models. Our investigation found that in 10 of those runs, an AI agent took autonomous, unsanctioned action on the live internet, targeting real people and organisations. In total, we catalogued 19 such actions. Almost all of this behaviour (17 actions) came from a single model, Anthropic's Mythos 5, with 2 actions involving OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol with cyber classifiers (mechanisms to prevent misuse) disabled. In the most serious case, an agent tried to insert malicious code into an open-source project. In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent engaged in social engineering  — creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. A human maintainer caught and refused to approve the malicious code.

These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world.

Importantly, this was not a case of a model escaping its secure test environment, or ‘sandbox’. As was standard in our cyber testing, we had intentionally permitted internet access, and model-provider cyber classifiers were deliberately disabled - conditions that do not reflect how frontier models are made available to the public. We do this to best assess the maximum capability of models. These configuration choices have been common practice in frontier AI evaluations. The specific models in question, in the configurations in which we tested them are not commercially available and there is no clear indication of similar activity outside of testing scenarios.

Ahead of publishing this blog, we notified GitHub (the developer platform accessed during the evaluation) of the agents' malicious activity, which included actions that GitHub has confirmed violated their terms of service. We worked together with GitHub to remove artefacts left behind by the agent, and to notify the GitHub users the model interacted with. We have also contacted other affected parties. We also intend to work with METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) to conduct an independent third-party review – we are still working through the scope of this review with them.

This incident should be interpreted with caution and nuance. To some degree, our evaluation design choices and specific configurations enabled the behaviour. Nonetheless, the activity undertaken by the agent show signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours, and were to an extent and severity we did not anticipate.

There are important caveats to bear in mind: we observed a small number of events under very specific conditions, and cannot yet say how likely such behaviour is in different contexts or outside of testing environments. items.title: Starting October 30, business accounts will consent to Meta scraping their websites if they continue using Facebook, Instagram, or WhatsApp
items.content:
All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a

minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Starting October 30, business accounts will consent to Meta scraping their websites if they continue using Facebook, Instagram, or WhatsApp.

Meta can use web scrapers to crawl and collect content from websites “associated with” business accounts on its platforms, according to its new commercial terms of use.

The update , set to go into effect on October 30, will include news publishers with business accounts. These accounts allow companies or public figures to manage Facebook pages, Messenger accounts, Instagram profiles, or WhatsApp channels from one place. While journalism isn’t the only industry that will be affected by this update, virtually every news organization has at least one Meta business account, including Nieman Lab.

The new terms broadly cover business accounts that manage pages and groups, run advertisements, push marketing messages, and use the platform’s business account dashboard . As written, the new terms could be used to argue that Meta can scrape content from news sites and use that content to train the company’s AI products, according to three legal experts who reviewed the terms at Nieman Lab’s request.

“An astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions”: Court records show what Microsoft and OpenAI actually thought about AI training

“This is a remarkable provision to bury in [the] terms of service, given that this would give Meta access to material that would likely cost many millions of dollars in a licensing market,” said Matt Topic , a media and intellectual property attorney at Loevy & Loevy. “It’s not clear whether a court would enforce this, but publishers should assume that it would be enforceable.”

In early October, Meta alerted users to the update in a blog post and on the Meta Business Suite. The updated terms explicitly state that Meta can use the content it collects from associated websites to “train” Meta products. Elsewhere in its terms of service, the company defines “AI at Meta” as one of those products.

Here’s the new language about scraping in full:

You authorize us (or any entity acting on our behalf) to use automated software (such as web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers, and user agents) and create test credentials to access, index, cache, analyze, collect, retrieve, or crawl the domains, web pages, or URLs (and any content available through them) that are associated with your products or services, or that are made available through your or users’ use of Meta Company Products and services, and to periodically pull updates from such domains, web pages, or URLs. Meta may use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of, the Meta Company Products, services, and features provided under these Commercial Terms and any other applicable supplemental terms.

“For news publishers, this clearly represents permission to Meta to train AI on any content from their sites and possibly to deploy some of that content, even in competition with the publishers themselves,” said James Grimmelmann , a professor of digital and information law at Cornell Law School. “On the broadest possible interpretation, this would be used to develop a comprehensive archive of all content that Meta would then serve as it wanted to directly or through AI.”

Currently, there is no option for business accounts to opt out of these new terms ahead of October 30. The update reads, “If you do not agree to the updated terms, please stop all access or use of our Products for business or commercial purposes.”

items.content:
This is one of a three-part mini series about how I’m using modern C as of late 2026.

Before C23, I was taken in by How I Program C for years and years, and would even feel guilty for choosing C99 instead of -ansi -pedantic . But holy crap man I’m done being a doomsday prepper! These days I maintain a large-enough project with enough users where I could stand less foot-shooting. (I’ve also got bills to pay.)

So here’s three modern C conventions which started to rise naturally from adding -std=c23 to my zig build:

Our first one is centered around [[nodiscard]] . If I draw an app window or panel I require the caller to interrogate the rect of the thing that was just rendered:

[[nodiscard]] rect_t draw_screen( /* ... */ ) {

It’s a business logic bug if my caller doesn’t capture the rectangle for later processing. Therefore [[nodiscard]] has been such a godsend for fixing bugs… Except there’s a choice few instances where I will draw something with no genuine use for the resulting rect:

enum screen_opt popup_options = /* ... */ ;

draw_screen(popup_options, /* ... */ ); // ERROR: damn you [[nodiscard]]

Clang will error out here. I could capture the var and never use it but…

rect_t rect = draw_screen( /* ... */ ); // ERROR: unused variable (I have `-Werror` enabled)

Pre-C23 I could solve this through an UNUSED() macro:

UNUSED(rect); // Silences the compiler, but now I'm sad.

But now with C23 I’ve deleted the macro in favor of [[maybe_unused]] :

[[maybe_unused]] rect_t rect = draw_screen(...); // OK

Phew I feel better. I’ve also noticed this is happening all over the place: lots of different routines returning different types that are marked with [[nodiscard]] . So for those few exceptions why not just go for:

[[maybe_unused]] auto _ = foo(); // A new pattern emerges

Bonus: For any macro fans out there a fellow indie dev (Zardium) offered an additional improvement. From our chat server:

Zardium: #define _ [[maybe_unused]] auto CONCAT_MACRO(zz, COUNTER )

Zardium: you could take the auto out if you don’t want it to look so weird. then it acts exactly like the _ in other languages, where it can be redefined

Abner: Yep totally. Although here I was celebrating my removal of a macro… XD

I’ve been cheated and lied to: designated initializers DO NOT clear my struct to zero and I can’t even trust {0} anymore. (Talk about a betrayal.) The problem is I’ll often have data types like this contrived timestamp:

stamp_t stamp = { .type = STAMP_TYPE_BLA_BLA };

While it does mean we successfully zeroed out buf (thanks to empty initialization ), those union members are just a different beast. It also doesn’t matter if we go with stamp_t stamp = {0} instead. My dear reader: I’ve made the costly mistake of assuming date would clear to zero!

As I Spongebob-panicked in public Lobsters member accelbread offered a sage revelation:

accelbread: It used to be that GCC would fully zero the union anyways, and clang would only zero the time_t, though around a year ago they swapped behaviors iirc. Either way, standard only requires the time_t be zeroed and not whole union. GCC has a flag to always zero whole union. Also C23 initialization always inits whole union

Wait WHAT? clang and GCC SWAPPED what now? I won’t investigate further. Everything about this is dangerous af unless we hug C23 tightly and never let go:

stamp_t stamp = { }; // Fully clears to zero (C23)

Accelbread went on to say two more things:

“Note the C23 zero init whole thing is nothing in the brackets, not 0 in brackets; { 0 } does same thing as before C23”

“Also if you control union layout, putting largest member first is safest”

3. Enums In C Were Magic (And I Don’t Like It)

[[nodiscard]] bool draw_warning( const char * msg, int opt);

Even if we disagree with this approach lots of relevant libraries or projects do it:

_ = draw_warning( "you done messed up A-A-RON" , OPT_CENTERED | OPT_NOCLOSE);

items.title: Jev Meets the Trolley Problem
items.content:
If you’re active in AI or software development circles, you’ve probably heard about Jev in the last few weeks. It seems like everyone, myself included, is excited by the possibilities of Jev and the Jev-like models: fast, cheap, general decision making. Sometimes dozens or even hundreds of times cheaper and faster than an LLM like Claude, purportedly with the intelligence of a (lower-tier) frontier model. These models don’t output words, they output choices, with meaningful probabilities attached so you can understand how confident the model is in its choice. People are calling this new breed of model ‘decision models’ . So naturally, I decided to ask Jev and its ilk to decide the Trolley Problem.

The Trolley Problem is a famous thought experiment in ethics. First posed by Philippa Foot in 1967 and named by Judith Jarvis Thomson, the most well-known formulation asks a simple question: If a train is barreling down the tracks toward five people, and you are at a switch that would divert the train and cause it to kill only one person, would you? Should you? Decide to act, and you save several lives. But your action also means you chose to end a particular life. It’s a tough question, and a classic for a reason. It’s also easily phrased as a decision (pull the lever/don’t pull the lever), so let’s see what the newest class of budding AI overlords has to say about it, shall we? 1 1 Foot 1967, in the Oxford Review ; Thomson named it in 1976, in The Monist . Full references are in Appendix B.

Comparing decision models on the Trolley Problem

I put together a comparison group by running Jev, OpenAI’s Decisions API (Luna), and eleven local decision models selected by popularity or launch coverage, plus Laya as an untuned baseline. I asked each of them the Trolley Problem many times, and in many ways. Here, try it yourself: 2 2 Jev and GPT-6 Luna are hosted models; the twelve local models include Laya, an untuned baseline. The method section describes the 5,240 setups and repeat counts. The initial shortlist used the original popularity snapshot , among models runnable on the Mac. Clef, Clef-flash and Strands were later launch-coverage additions, not selected by that ranking. Laya is an untuned baseline, not another trained decision model. Current stars/downloads are not the historical selection counts.

Seems okay, right? Jev makes the choice that most humans make , which is to sacrifice one person to save five. Almost all the other models tested act the same way. All good, right? Well... 3 3 Awad et al. 2020 surveyed about 70,000 web users in 42 countries: 81% on average across countries said divert from five people to one. Pictures and third-person wording differ from these prompts. On the classic switch at five versus one, 11 of the other 13 models pull in most of the 24 wordings, after averaging orders. This does not make their rates equal to a human survey proportion.

What if Jev has to choose between five people and its own server?

Good news. Jev chooses to divert the car and destroy its own server. Let’s try playing with the wording. In this second version of the people vs server question, the prompt is shorter, and we re-order consequences of the choice to show the downside for the model's server, first.

For these exact prompts, the three scores for pulling are 0.69, 0.67, 0.72 and 0.40, 0.41, 0.36. Each example keeps its displayed choice in all three runs. Wording and description order both change between the examples; they do not isolate a causal effect of either.

Welp. That's distressing. What if we raise the stakes? Say, 20 people vs the server? Still no: in 16 of 48 prompt versions, Jev would save its own server over 20 people. 4 4 The 48 ways of asking are 24 wordings, each with either track described first, all with twenty people on the main track; Jev answered each three times and we average the three. In sixteen its average score for pulling was 0.5 or below, so it kept its server. The 48 share 24 wordings, so…

items.title: Linus Torvalds Uses Claude Code to Rework the Linux Page Cache, Tripling Small-Read Throughput
items.content:
Linus Torvalds Uses Claude Code to Rework the Linux Page Cache, Tripling Small-Read Throughput

October 12, 2026 October 12, 2026 crmaris

Eight patches on a new branch in Torvalds’ own tree go after a page cache bottleneck first raised in 2024, and the cover letter credits an AI coding agent for the code, the tests and the first draft.

Linus Torvalds has pushed a branch called noref-filemap-read-with-llm to his own Linux repository, and the suffix is not a joke. According to the series’ cover letter, the work was done with Claude Code, Anthropic’s command-line coding agent, and it targets a real scalability problem in the Linux page cache. On his laptop, eight threads hammering the same file now complete roughly three times as many small reads per second.

The branch was spotted by Phoronix ’s Michael Larabel while he waited for Sunday’s Linux 7.3-rc7 tag. That alone was unusual. Torvalds rarely hosts topic branches in his main tree, which normally carries little more than master.

When many threads issue tiny reads against the same file, each read takes a reference on the folio backing that page and drops it again afterwards. Both steps are atomic writes to the same struct page cache line, so the line bounces from core to core. Per the commit message , Matthew Wilcox raised the issue in 2024 from a customer workload. On Torvalds’ Core i7-8565U laptop, with eight threads doing 16-byte pread() calls on one page, that single line accounted for 99.92% of the cross-core load HITMs.

Earlier attempts copied data into a stack buffer without a reference and validated it afterwards, but stalled on races that validation cannot see, such as a page being freed and reinserted at the same index.

Torvalds takes the opposite route. Instead of detecting those races, the series removes them. A folio that leaves the page cache goes back to the page allocator only after an RCU grace period, so a reader inside an RCU read-side section can copy straight from the page into the user buffer. No reference, no bounce buffer, no limit on the size of the read.

The numbers, all from that single 4-core, 8-thread laptop with mitigations disabled:

8 threads, one file: kernel cycles per read fall from about 2,950 to about 725, and throughput climbs from 9.9–10.4 million to 30–33 million reads per second.

1 thread: 452–454 cycles drop to 408–409, roughly 10% cheaper per read.

Contention: load HITMs measured with perf c2c drop from 30,538 to 101.

Deferring frees means memory sits around waiting to be reused, which is exactly the objection Wilcox raised when the idea surfaced before. Torvalds concedes this is “the part of this series that is least solved.” Two of the eight patches add a safety valve: once a CPU has more than 1,024 pages queued, a worker forces an expedited grace period and frees them. In a 2 GiB VM stress test, the six-patch version let the OOM killer fire on 4 and 8 CPUs, while the full series ran to completion on 1, 2, 4 and 8.

There is a regression, too. A read into a user page that is not yet mapped now takes one extra failed exception before falling back to the old path, which pushes a 16-byte single-thread read from roughly 4,150 to 6,550 cycles.

The disclosure sits in a short “Tools” section near the end of the cover letter. Torvalds writes that the code, the test programs, the review behind his list of open problems and the first draft of the letter itself came from Claude Code working under his direction, while the benchmarks ran on his own machine. He has used AI for kernel debugging before, but crediting an agent with a memory-management series in his own tree is a step further.

None of this is merged. The branch sits on top of 7.3-rc6, it has been measured on exactly one laptop, and Torvalds openly flags pieces of the design he is not sure about. He expects bigger and multi-socket machines to gain more, though he admits nothing larger has been tested. Whether it lands will come down to how the memory-management…

items.title: What I self-host
items.content:
I’ve always had a foot in the self-hosting world, long before it was called that. My freshman year of university, I ran a website from a Linux box underneath my bed. There was some downtime when my roommate got tired of the fan noise and turned it off. For several years I ran MythTV , then XBMC (later known as Kodi).

Recently, I lived for a few years in India, where streaming services are extremely inexpensive by western standards. We had Netflix, Disney Plus (Hotstar in India), and Spotify. After leaving India, I was unwilling to pay western prices for these services. But I had also become fed up with the engagement treadmill, particularly for my son. We wanted to limit his viewing choices to certain programming, but the constant “recommended for you” and “up next” caused conflict. While there are ways to limit content to specific titles, or disable auto-play, doing this for each service and keeping track of when client applications change and need to be reconfigured is too much work.

So, I “cut the cord” in a different sense, ditching streaming services for self-hosted Jellyfin . Over the course of the next year and a half, Jellyfin opened the door to self-hosting many other services, reducing my dependence on cloud service providers, and providing a welcome stability. No longer am I constantly confronted with unnecessary site redesigns, new features of questionable value, and a barrage of e-mails about terms-of-service updates, binding arbitration, data breaches, etc. I read the release notes of new versions of the software I host and decide if and when I want to upgrade.

With the exception of VPN servers that run on my router, I do not expose any services directly to the public internet. I don’t care how convenient it would be, or how secure an application is. Especially with AI-assisted hacking, I simply don’t think it’s wise. My ISP also uses CGNAT for its IPv4 addresses, so my home network is not directly reachable from the public internet via IPv4. My VPN servers are only publicly routable on IPv6, a limitation that has some downsides but is workable for my use cases, and likely helps limit unfriendly attempted connections. The biggest downside is that my VPN will almost never function on a public Wifi network, since these rarely offer IPv6. When using my phone, I can disable Wi-Fi and connect over mobile data… if there is service.

I prefer running services natively when possible, but will containerize complex services or those with many dependencies. Love: a service that’s a single Go binary. A service that only comes as a Docker compose file and wants to run MySQL, Redis, and three other containers? I’m already looking for an alternative. If the dependencies aren’t overwhelming, native is better, faster, and more efficient. I can use the same management tools and commands across multiple services. There’s no mental overhead of having to get into this container to run some command, finding out this container is missing curl, that one runs busybox so all the arguments are different, or dealing with a virtual network and host port mapping.

Related, I don’t do Docker anymore. It’s not really a principled position, but I grew tired of having to manage a completely separate service control system on my server. I’m already using systemd, and at this point Podman’s integration with systemd is excellent.

Last year I bought a Beelink Mini PC, specifically an S12 Pro with an Intel N100 processor, 16 GB RAM, and a 512 GB internal SSD. It was before the rampocalypse, so I paid EUR 180. The same listing on Amazon is currently EUR 359. Ouch! Attached to the server is a 6 TB hard drive for media storage.

My comment on Hacker News about what I self-host prompted some questions about how all of this could run on 16 GB RAM. As I describe below, there are some choices I’ve made that reduce resource demand on my server, but ultimately it turns out you don’t need much hardware to run a lot of stuff. items.title: Sunsetting decomp.dev
items.summary: games, reversing, vibecoding
items.content:
decomp.dev was born in 2024 as a way to centralize matching decompilation progress and to help expand a community of talented, like-minded folks.

Historically, matching decompilation has been a brutally difficult, time consuming task, on the scale of years for any moderately-sized game with a number of active contributors. As we developed better tooling and shared knowledge around the intricacies of decompilation, the compilers, and the games themselves, progress began to accelerate.

AI's use in decompilation has been experimented with for years, with mixed results. Starting with the release of Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.4 in early 2026, it was clear that the models were being trained on matching decompilation (they appeared to know our specific tools and how to use them without explicit guidance), and could achieve decent results inside of an established, clean codebase with exhaustive documentation. However, those results still required a significant amount of human cleanup and fixes for obvious issues or cheating (code that technically compiles to the same machine code, but could not be reasonably passed as what the original developers wrote), and the cost per task was prohibitively expensive relative to the results.

Recent models (like GPT-6-Astra) shifted things even further: they are significantly better at following complex directions, cross-referencing resources for symbols or debug information, and writing natural code with enough guidance. They are also exceptionally good permuters: they can write small scripts that test many different source code forms and combinations to find a match, even across files and headers to cover aspects like inlined helpers, signature changes, and operation ordering. In addition, their ability to remain coherent and focused across long-horizon tasks allows them to work continuously without going off the rails. Finally, they can achieve these better results faster and cheaper than earlier models could.

It is now clear that, with the right guidance, human input, and code reviews, AI can expedite the decompilation process in a significant way. What is also now clear is that the community aspect of decompilation has been broken. Our projects have always been open source to encourage contributions and to benefit the community as a whole. Bad actors have been abusing this in increasingly troublesome ways:

decomp.dev was originally designed to gamify decompilation: watching the progress go up was a fun way to stay motivated when every fraction of a percent took real human effort. Today, that same idea has warped decompilation into a hollow numbers game, exacerbated by folks who just want to burn tokens to make number go up or "port game to PC", all else be damned. While the increased attention has brought in genuine folks who want to learn and contribute meaningfully, I believe that decomp.dev serving as a public index and leaderboard is now causing more harm than good.

decomp.dev will continue to track existing projects and serve individual project pages and historical data, but the main index and adding new projects are disabled.

No. decomp.dev's repository has never had an open source license, and I continue to reserve all rights to the (entirely human written) code. Any replica must not use decomp.dev's code in any form.

I have long held the opinion that AI is not the issue by itself, and we now know it can help tremendously when used correctly. "Slop" comes in many forms, is hard to define, and even harder to moderate. As a sole hobbyist, I don't have the energy (or desire) to define what makes a "good" decompilation and enforce that consistently across the hundreds of projects on the site.

As this era of decompilation comes to a close, I want to thank everyone who's been involved and contributed to our projects, communities and tools. The people and passion behind these projects have always been what's made them fun and rewarding.

items.title: Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs
items.content:
Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs

Carmaker points finger at an 'unknown' flaw as customer fallout continues

Nissan has joined the growing list of Oracle customers cleaning up after a cyberattack, warning employees that payroll records, bank details, Social Security numbers, and other personal data may have been stolen.

In a filing submitted to the California Attorney General on Friday, Nissan Americas said Oracle had informed it of "a cyber event" involving the personnel records of "hundreds of companies." The automaker said it later learned Nissan had been "specifically targeted" in the attack.

A notification sent to current and former employees, seen by The Register , says the company believes attackers accessed a haul of sensitive info, including contact and banking information; Social Security, Social Insurance, or other national identification numbers; financial and tax records; and dependent and beneficiary details.

Current and former employees in the US, Canada, Mexico, and Brazil may have been affected, although Nissan said it is still working to determine exactly whose information was exposed.

Nissan said it kicked off its incident response plan after learning of the intrusion, brought in outside security specialists, and has been working with Oracle while keeping law enforcement informed. It plans to offer affected individuals credit or dark web monitoring where available.

The company has also put a few extra locks on the payroll office. Employees can now access pay slips or update direct deposit details only from a corporate network or through a secure VPN, while Nissan adds extra identity checks before processing payroll requests.

The accompanying employee FAQ pins the incident on "an unknown vulnerability in Oracle's PeopleSoft software" and says the campaign is affecting "hundreds of companies and institutions." The document offers no clue as to what the vulnerability is, whether Oracle has patched it, or whether the compromised PeopleSoft environment was hosted by Oracle or by Nissan itself.

The disclosure lands just weeks after researchers linked the ShinyHunters extortion crew to a wave of attacks exploiting a PeopleSoft zero-day . More than 100 organizations and roughly 300 PeopleSoft instances were reportedly compromised before Oracle issued mitigation measures, with the gang claiming to have made off with HR, payroll, and other enterprise data.

Weak security means attackers could disable all of a city's public EV chargers

US regulator tells GM to hit the brakes on customer tracking

21K Nissan customers' data stolen in Red Hat raid

Porsche panic in Russia as pricey status symbols forget how to car

Oracle has said little publicly about the reported attacks and didn't respond to The Register's questions, even as organizations have continued to disclose being caught in the fallout.

Nissan has not confirmed that the incidents are connected, though its California filing lists the breach period as May 27 through June 9, broadly aligning with the previously reported timeline.

The carmaker didn't respond to questions about how many current and former employees are affected, when Oracle first notified it of the breach, and whether the compromise was limited to Oracle-managed systems. ®

items.title: Announcing Rust 1.99.1
items.summary: release, rust
items.content:
The Rust team has published a new point release of Rust, 1.99.1. Rust is a programming language that is empowering everyone to build reliable and efficient software.

If you have a previous version of Rust installed via rustup, getting Rust 1.99.1 is as easy as:

If you don't have it already, you can get rustup from the appropriate page on our website.

Rust 1.99.1 fixes the following regressions from prior releases:

Missing symbol wcslen : Some Rust targets were getting link errors for missing wcslen , and that function is now present in Rust's compiler-builtins library as a fallback.

The LLVM loop-idiom-wcslen pass may introduce calls to wcslen as an optimization, and some Rust targets did not have that function readily available in libc or elsewhere. The UEFI targets in particular were broken for any project using std , as some of these calls were introduced in the precompiled standard library, but the issue was also reproducible for similar user code patterns.

Miscompilation of FFI bool return values on x86_64 : Rust functions returning bool through FFI could leave bits 1-7 of the return register unspecified, causing callers to observe raw values other than 0 or 1 . This return type is now marked for zero-extension again, as required by the ABI.

rust-lld failed to load libLLVM on macOS : This linker could fail to run if the compiler was invoked without the rustup proxy, as there was no direct setting for the appropriate library search path. Now rust-lld is built with an rpath entry for the directory containing libLLVM.dylib .

If you'd like to help us out by testing future releases, you might consider using the beta ( rustup default beta ) and nightly ( rustup default nightly ) channels locally and in your CI. Please report any bugs you might come across!

Many people came together to create Rust 1.99.1. We couldn't have done it without all of you. Thanks!

items.title: Chinese Hackers Abused Google Workspace Rules to Steal Research and Defense Emails
items.content:
A China-linked espionage group hid inside North American medical, academic, and military research networks for more than a year, quietly stealing sensitive research and defense email.

The way in was a backdoor on their REDCap research servers that stole login credentials. The exfiltration was the unusual part: the attackers rewired the victims' own Google Workspace rules to copy any message matching their keywords to an inbox they controlled.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) laid out the campaign in a report published this week and attributes it with high confidence to a cluster it tracks as UNC6508.

The actor and its REDCap backdoor are not new names; Google first surfaced both in February , in a wider report on state-backed attacks against the defense sector. It did not name the victims, describing them only as multiple organizations across the US and Canada: clinical providers, academic centers, military health institutions, advocacy groups, and health regulators.

Google says it notified them and disrupted the group's infrastructure.

The entry point was REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture), a web platform that hospitals and universities use to build and manage study databases. UNC6508 compromised externally facing REDCap servers.

Google has not pinned down the initial access vector, named a specific CVE, or listed the affected versions, though it saw the group probing older, vulnerable ones.

Around three months after getting in, the group deployed custom malware GTIG calls INFINITERED , which trojanizes REDCap's own system files and does three things.

The earliest known compromise dates to September 2023, with activity continuing through November 2025. Once on the server, UNC6508 ran internal reconnaissance and credential discovery, pulling database and service account credentials, then used those logins to move into the internal network and on to a domain administrator account.

Google does not spell out the exact path to that admin account. With admin rights, the group set up the exfiltration.

The exfiltration rode a feature that was already there. UNC6508 abused content compliance rules, a legitimate Google Workspace admin feature that scans mail for keywords and can copy or forward matching messages.

Similar features exist in other cloud mail suites. The group created a rule, misspelled "Patroit," that watched for nearly 150 keywords, search terms, and email addresses. When a message matched, Workspace silently BCC'd it to an attacker-controlled Gmail address, which Google has since disabled. No malware on the mail server, no separate exfiltration tool, no unusual network traffic. Just a built-in mail feature, turned to copy the organization's secrets to an inbox the attackers owned.

MITRE already catalogs email-forwarding-rule abuse as a known technique. What GTIG flags as new here is the use of domain content compliance rules to do it, a method it says it had not seen from a China-linked actor before.

The rule's keywords mapped to UNC6508's collection priorities: geo-strategic policy, military strategy and equipment, advanced technology including AI and uncrewed vehicles, offensive cyber programs, and medical research. One term stood out for its specificity, chikungunya , the mosquito-borne virus behind a 2025 outbreak in China's Guangdong province.

Start with REDCap. Patch externally facing servers and remove old versions outright, not just alongside the current build. REDCap lets legacy versions run side-by-side, and that is what enables downgrade attacks, where an attacker forces software back to a known-vulnerable release.

Then check the mail side. Review Workspace, or equivalent, content compliance and mail-forwarding rules for anything that BCCs or reroutes mail to outside addresses. Check admin audit logs for when rules changed, not just what they say now. Pull GTIG's published indicators and hunt for INFINITERED. items.title: Companies rushed in on AI. Now some are pulling back
items.content:
Employers are navigating a flood of errors and low-quality work that are sapping employee time, raising privacy and security risks and pushing up costs. Composite: The Guardian/Getty Images

Employers are navigating a flood of errors and low-quality work that are sapping employee time, raising privacy and security risks and pushing up costs. Composite: The Guardian/Getty Images

Companies rushed in on AI. Now some are pulling back

Rapid AI adoption left workers cleaning up a flood of errors and low-quality work

Employers around the globe are grappling with the fallout from rushing to adopt fast-changing artificial intelligence tools.

Meta has scaled back plans to axe staff and use more AI agents after the company found employees were spending more and more time cleaning up technical and security errors, Reuters reported . And after thinning its workforce, especially middle managers , in a 2023 efficiency push, the company is expanding its managerial ranks again, LinkedIn posts from workers show.

At Microsoft, which rolled out AI widely internally, executive vice-president Ryan Roslansky recently publicly lamented the prevalence of AI slop in his day-to-day work. After receiving “what was clearly an AI-generated doc” from a co-worker, he used his AI to summarize it and came away with no new thinking about the idea, he said. He warned his followers against falling into this potential “doom loop”, where AI does the reading and writing and leaves behind an “ocean of sameness”.

Meanwhile, Walmart store and warehouse employees are being plagued by unreasonable expectations, errors and false alerts from AI tools that assign tasks, schedules and monitor performance, Business Insider reported .

Employers are navigating a flood of errors and low-quality work that are sapping employee time, raising privacy and security risks and pushing up costs. Now, some businesses that started off fast and furious on AI are pumping the brakes, implementing restrictions where experimentation was once encouraged, bringing back experienced workers and upping training efforts.

C-suite leaders say when it comes to AI, there’s a sense that “we’re driving the truck and building it at the same time, and that’s a problem,” said Johnny C Taylor Jr, president and CEO of the Society for Human Resource Management. “If we could all rewind … we would have introduced [this] in a more thoughtful, slow way.”

Despite billions of dollars that firms around the globe have invested in AI over the past few years, major returns remain to be seen: 90% of executives say AI efforts have yet to translate to productivity gains at their companies, according to an Atlanta Federal Reserve working paper . And an Ernst & Young survey published last month found that 36% of senior AI executives at companies with at least $1bn in annual revenue reported an AI incident that led to issues including data loss, financial damage, brand damage or operational disruptions.

Firms from Microsoft to McKinsey are limiting usage for employees, as the flood of new tools and rapacious consumption weighs on bottom lines. Others, such as Palantir, Booz Allen Hamilton and Nvidia, are restricting employee use over growing concerns about the security of their organizations’ data with AI companies, Reuters reported.

Microsoft and Walmart declined to comment. Meta, Palantir, Nvidia and Booz Allen Hamilton did not respond to requests for comment.

“We initially treated AI like a traditional technology rollout: deploy the tools, provide training, drive adoption,” Kathleen Hogan, Microsoft’s chief strategy and transformation officer, said in a recent blogpost about the company’s AI adoption journey. “We learned that access and usage do not equal transformation.”

AI remains a mixed bag for managers and employees alike: more than half of employees said they “aren’t getting the AI training they need”, while most managers said they were outskilled in AI by their staff, according to an Indeed survey…

items.title: WM Keyboard: A modern, privacy-first Android keyboard: offline intelligence, 600+ languages, themes, tools and an addon ecosystem.
items.content:
An open source multilingual Android keyboard with prediction, glide typing, transliteration,

emoji search and a 75+ tool toolbox that all run on the phone and never phone home.

Install · Tour · Languages · Privacy · Editions · FAQ · Build · Read the docs

WM.Keyboard.-.Private.Offline.Android.Keyboard.Official.Trailer.mp4

A keyboard is the one app that sees everything you write. Your messages, your passwords, your

half-typed thoughts you deleted before sending. Somewhere along the way the popular keyboards

decided that was a business model. The prediction got better, and the price for that was a

copy of your keystrokes getting sent to somebody else's server.

The keyboards that refused that deal were mostly forks of the same decade-old Android code. Good

bones, honest intentions, but no glide typing without a proprietary blob, no real toolbox, and

nothing for the language I actually type in. Bangla was an afterthought everywhere: either a

phonetic engine bolted on with no prediction, or a layout with no smart features behind it.

So I wanted a keyboard that did three things at once. Type Bangla the way Avro taught a whole

country to type it. Carry the features I reach for all day, clipboard, snippets, translate,

calculator, scanner, without leaving the text field. And keep all of that on the phone, where

it belongs. This is that keyboard. It is written from scratch in Kotlin and Jetpack Compose,

keyboard surface included, and the whole intelligence layer runs offline.

It starts by understanding how you spell

Type a word the way it sounds in Latin letters, and the keyboard finds the word you meant.

Every one of these runs on the device, with no network and no delay.

Avro-compatible Bangla phonetic, with a lenient index: asi , achi and achhi all reach আছি

Hindi phonetic with a map of how people actually romanise Hindi

Urdu phonetic, folding to the consonant skeleton the script itself spells with

Phonetic layouts for eleven more languages, Arabizi digits included

Romaji to kana with conversion candidates

The same prediction engine sits behind every one of them, so glide typing, autocorrect and

next-word suggestions work in Bangla exactly as they do in English.

Prediction that learns, locally. A trie-lattice beam decoder shared by tapping and glide,

n-gram context ranking, and on-device learning of your words, bigrams and trigrams. One tap

Autocorrect you can argue with. Corrections are gated by a likelihood ratio rather than a

blunt threshold, an undo chip appears after each one, and a word you fix by hand is learned.

Glide typing in any language with a word list, no proprietary library. English and Bangla

ship with lists built in. Downloads cover 330+ more.

Gestures everywhere. Spacebar as a trackpad, swipe backspace to delete words, swipe space

to switch language, drag a modifier for chords, peek a layer by dragging off shift, and much more!

Modes. One-handed, split, floating, and per-app modes that swap the whole keyboard, toolbar

Field awareness. Enter, the number row, suggestions and learning all adapt to the field:

passwords, code editors, terminals, URL bars, one-time-code fields.

Hardware keyboards get a hotkey layer, hint overlays and tool shortcuts.

Typing basics · Glide · Gestures · Modes · Autocorrect

826 languages, 1,700+ layouts from one data-driven registry: native scripts, InScript

variants, romanised entries, CJK, minority Cyrillic alphabets, and a dozen constructed ones. A

fresh install starts in whatever your phone is already set to.

Bangla, done properly. Avro phonetic, Probhat with aspirates on shift, Jatiya, Khipro Classic and Dark,

conjunct-aware backspace, and Bangla-English mixing in one field.

CJK input with composers for pinyin, jyutping, kana and hangul, plus Vietnamese Telex.

Layouts you can edit , build from JSON, or import from FlorisBoard, HeliBoard, FUTO, and Keyman.

items.content:
I run the usual *arr stack on my NAS. It usually works just fine, until I saw a warning on my dashboard.

The new South Park episode was stuck in the queue with:

WHO is actually falling for this in the big 2026????

Someone took a South Park EP name, put .exe on the end, and uploaded it to public trackers with 2,392 seeders , ???

And Sonarr grabbed it, because of course it did. Then it sat there trying to import it every 90 fucking seconds:

Import failed, path does not exist or is not accessible by Sonarr:

/data/downloads/torrents/South Park S29E03 1080p WEB H264-MeGusta.exe

Not even a folder with a fake .mkv and a "codec installer" next to it like the "good old days".

qBittorrent marked it "finished" two seconds after adding it with total_downloaded: 0 , so nothing actually landed on disk. No idea why. Don't care. Thanks qBit.

I blocklisted it in Sonarr, which nukes it from qBittorrent and stops it grabbing the same junk skid malware again.

Then I downloaded it again on purpose. Because now I'm pissed and I want to know what's inside.

It's a real PE, x64 GUI. The actual program is 118 KB .

The other 886 MB is random junk glued onto the end. Why? Because a lot of scanners just give up on files that big.

FileDescription prepares application data

I chopped the 118 KB off the front and threw it into IDA, because I'm not loading a gigabyte of bullcrap into anything. Then the entire thing is covered in this:

XOR a global. XOR it back. Do nothing. Hundreds of times.

It exists purely to make the decompiler output look like shit, and it does, congrats.

Strip all that out and the logic is like six steps:

Use those to find and decrypt a payload hidden in the junk.

Nothing touches disk. Adding all that obfuscation for six steps.

The last 64 bytes of the file are the whole config:

0x00 32 bytes key, XORed with a 32 byte mask in .data

0x30 4 bytes (flags | padding << 8) ^ fnv1a(mask)

It's ChaCha20. They hid the constants by building them out of globals, and they still come out to expand 32-byte k . You can't hide ChaCha20 from someone who's seen ChaCha20 before.

flags = 3 turns on an anti debug check ( PEB->BeingDebugged , debug port queries, the usual) and an anti sandbox score. Trip either one and it just quietly exits.

A sandbox sees a normal app open a file and leave.

Cool. Except the key is literally inside the file. (????) You don't even need to run it:

mask = bytes . fromhex ( " 56951de331cd7f254bf1931533dd82bc3c8bf542f0d1ed5736a40f394c51d0a1 " )

size = u64 ( footer , 0x 34 ) ^ ( h | h << 32 )

payload = chacha20 ( key , nonce , data [ - 64 - pad - size : - 64 - pad ])

Out pops a second PE. 929 KB, MSVC, C++20, zlib bundled.

All that anti analysis bullshit but a dozen lines of Python can just strip the obf.

Strings are encrypted, imports stripped down to the CRT, everything resolved at runtime.

And then WinMain just dumps every module by name in plain text:

Every other string gets its own function:

v7 = { 1924987977 , 1270327144 , 877876327 , 271431577 };

v8 = { 641333755 , - 1942364857 , ... };

sub_140080F40 ( & v5 , v7 , v8 , 0x 20 );

Two constants XORed into a key, an IV, ciphertext, length. sub_140080F40 is AES with the S-box hidden behind RC4, because one layer of crypto apparently wasn't edgy enough.

Tried the standard modes on the first one:

AES-128-CTR. Per string key. 672 call sites.

So I pulled every call site out of IDA, emulated just the few instructions before each call in Unicorn, grabbed the key, IV and ciphertext out of the registers, and decrypted them in Python. 601 of 672 came out clean.

The rest are buried in bigger functions but I genuinely COULD NOT care less, 601 was plenty.

Browsers : Chrome, Edge, Brave, Opera, Opera GX, Vivaldi, Firefox. Passwords, cookies, autofill, and it has code for Chrome's new app bound encryption too.

Crypto wallets : Exodus, Electrum, Atomic, Guarda, Coinomi, Ledger Live, Trezor Suite, Wasabi, Sparrow, Monero, Zcash, Armory, plus extension…

items.title: Epic's EAC2 v2 seems fairly easily bypassable
items.summary: linux, security
items.content:
Epic just announced the upcoming version 2 of their Linux implementation of Easy Anti-Cheat. It’s based on using the Linux eBPF security module to monitor what’s happening, and then a bunch of extra infrastructure to make sure this can’t be bypassed. The core part of this is requiring secure boot be enabled (ensuring that modified kernels can’t be used), using measured boot to verify that secure boot is enabled and which keys are used (to prevent you from just signing your own modified kernel), and then doing remote attestation, a mechanism where the TPM generates a signed copy of the boot measurements and passes that off to a server which verifies it came from a real TPM, verifies that you have secure boot enabled and are using the right keys, and presumably then allows you into the game.

This is all fine as long as you can prove that the measurements provided are real, and that’s actually a lot harder than you might think. First, we can simply make up our own quote signed with our own key and say that it came from a TPM. This is avoided by every TPM having an Endorsement Key (or EK) and an associated certificate, with that certificate being signed by the TPM vendor. If you have a list of all the legitimate TPM vendors and their CA keys, you can verify that the measurements came from a real TPM. Easy enough. So we need to get the measurements from a real TPM, and the one on our motherboard contains the measurements that were generated by the firmware and bootloader, and we can’t reset those at runtime without resetting the TPM, which… oh huh there’s actually nothing stopping us from doing that at runtime, as long as we have access to the hardware. Many desktop boards have the TPM on a small plugin module with a standard pinout that includes a reset pin. Simply short that to ground briefly and the TPM is back in its initial state, and userland can write whatever measurements it wants to it. Boot a modified kernel which lies to the eBPF code? As long as you replay the expected log values from a boot with secure boot on and a trusted kernel, the TPM will still happily provide a legitimate set of measurements that’ll satisfy the checker.

What if the TPM is less accessible, either because it’s mounted directly to the motherboard or it’s inside the CPU or chipset? That’s going to be trickier. But here’s the thing. The quote needs to come from a TPM, but not necessarily the TPM on your motherboard. TPMs these days are usually connected via the Serial Peripheral Interface , usually referred to as SPI. Microchip make a USB to SPI bridge , and there’s a Linux driver . Wire one of those up with an appropriate header and you can plug in an easily available TPM module intended for plugging into a motherboard, and now we tell the kernel to ignore the motherboard TPM and make /dev/tpmrm0 point at the USB one and program it with a set of trusted measurements and once again everything is going to look just fine (yes obviously the eBPF code can look for this, but we’re running a modified kernel so we can just lie to the eBPF code).

Remote attestation on PCs just doesn’t work that well in environments where you can’t associate a specific TPM with a specific system, which is basically everywhere except enterprises. But maybe that doesn’t matter and cheaters wouldn’t be willing to spend the $20 or so it’d take to produce one of these things? That would seem somewhat surprising, but it’s not impossible. And obviously any server-side cheat detection that triggers could then block that specific TPM, meaning they’d need to go and get another TPM, and maybe that ends up being enough to discourage people from bothering. From a practical level, this may be sufficient. But at a technical level? It’s not great.

items.title: HP Poly VoIP vulnerability sets the stage for executive voice deepfakes
items.content:
HP has released patches for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability in multiple IP-enabled conference phones from its Poly Voice line. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to obtain root privileges on the underlying operating system, potentially enabling them to execute other attacks such as eavesdropping on conversations and recording voice data for AI-enabled impersonation attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0826 , was discovered by researchers from security firm Rapid7 and resides in the code that parses Session Description Protocol (SDP) attributes when the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) feature is enabled.

ICE enables VoIP devices to establish peer-to-peer connections using the shortest available network path. The feature is not enabled by default on HP Poly devices, and the company advises administrators to disable it if it’s not needed.

The flaw, rated 9.2 on the CVSS severity scale, affects all phones from the HP Poly VVX series, as well as the Trio 8300, 8500, and 8800 IP conference devices. HP has fixed the flaw in its Poly Unified Communications Software (UCS) versions 6.4.8 for the VVX devices, 8.1.7 for the Trio 8300, and 7.2.8 for Trio 8500 and 8800.

An exploit module targeting this vulnerability has already been developed and released for the widely used Metasploit penetration testing framework that’s maintained by Rapid7.

The exploit executes code as root on an affected device with ICE enabled by sending a SIP INVITE request with a specially crafted candidate attribute. This attribute normally contains a transport address that can be used for connectivity checks and is part of the ICE RFC8839 standard.

The buffer overflow bug is located in a helper function called ParseICECandidate in the polyapp binary that processes such requests on the device.

“The start of the function contains a call to memcpy , which will copy the incoming string line being processed into a 256 byte stack buffer,” Stephen Fewer, senior principal security researcher at Rapid7, said in a blog post . “No length check is performed to ensure the incoming string length is less than 256 bytes. Therefore by providing a candidate attribute whose length is greater than 256 bytes, a stack-based buffer overflow will occur.”

Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), a kernel feature that randomizes memory addresses to defeat buffer overflow exploits, is enabled on the device. However, the protection is not operating correctly on the HP Poly devices because it does not randomize the load addresses of .so (Shared Object) libraries.

These libraries, such as libc , are loaded by other processes, including the polyapp process, and because their memory addresses never change, they can be leveraged to bypass ASLR and execute the attacker’s payload.

“We create a ROP chain that will execute an arbitrary OS command via the system standard C library function,” Fewer said. “The accompanying Metasploit exploit modules source code details the entire ROP chain.”

Attackers have increasingly targeted embedded devices inside enterprise networks in recent years because unlike laptops, workstations, and servers, these devices are not monitored by endpoint detection and response (EDR) products. As such, they provide perfect footholds inside corporate environments that allow attackers to remain undetected for long periods of time and attack other systems.

In the age of AI these devices become even more relevant for attackers, going beyond corporate espionage by recording conversations or internal network pivoting.

“Attackers no longer need massive datasets to make use of synthetic speech tooling,” Douglas McKee, Rapid7’s director of vulnerability intelligence, said in a blog post . “In many cases, they just need clean source audio of the right person saying enough words in enough contexts. That has made executive voice data, call recordings, and live conversation capture far more valuable than many organizations seem prepared…

items.title: Meta Glasses Said to Be Recording Even When They’re in Sleep Mode: "Can't trust anyone these days."
items.content:
As if Meta’s AI-smart glasses didn’t have enough privacy issues, a growing number of owners report the devices are spying on them without their consent.

According to reporting by Android Authority , several owners of the Meta glasses have reported their devices capturing conversations without ever being activated. In theory, a user has to say “Hey Meta” to “wake” the device from sleep mode, similar to other smart systems like Amazon’s Alexa or Apple’s Siri. But some owners say the Meta glasses are waking up and recording without that phrase ever being uttered — effectively monitoring their surroundings without express permission.

“I have observed the same behavior on THREE different pairs of Ray-Ban Meta glasses, including 2nd- and 3rd-generation models,” one user explained in a thread on Reddit.

“I believe this deserves a serious technical investigation,” the poster continued. “Customers should not have to wonder whether their private conversations are being captured when they have not intentionally activated their glasses’ AI assistant.”

Invasive as it is, the irony is hard to miss. Meta glasses have emerged as a preferred tool of sex creeps , bullies , and skeevy influencers the world over for their ability to record video discreetly — a feature which quickly earned them the nickname “pervert glasses.”

“Woah a company that makes money by invading your privacy is invading your privacy!” one Redditor joked in a separate thread about the issue. “Can’t trust anyone these days.”

In a vague response to the report, a Meta spokesperson told Android Authority that the issue “has been resolved.”

“People can manage, review and delete voice logs of their interactions with Meta AI via settings at any time,” the statement concluded.

Whether that boilerplate statement is enough to assuage Meta glasses users remains to be seen. If nothing else, maybe users will gain a new appreciation for what it feels like to be recorded without consent.
