Forgejo version 17.0 was released on 15 October 2026. Forgejo is a lightweight, community-developed, self-hosted platform for code collaboration.

This article contains a selection of the changes that were introduced. A complete list of changes is available in the release notes .

A dedicated test instance is available to try it out. Before upgrading, it is strongly recommended to make a full backup as explained in the upgrade guide and carefully read all breaking changes from the release notes .

If in doubt, do not hesitate to ask for help in the chat room .

In rendered documents, absolute links to resources inside a repository are now resolved with respect to the root of the repository. !12939

This is a breaking change from the previous behaviour when these links were rendered using the root of the instance. Absolute links in issue and pull request descriptions and comments remain rendered with respect to the instance’s root. !13993

This change increases the compatibility with other Git forges and thus, makes migrations to Forgejo even easier.

Deprecation of action run webhook events

Action run webhook events are replaced by the more capable and less problematic workflow run events. !14351 The action run events have been deprecated for removal in a future Forgejo version. Unfortunately, it is not possible to migrate existing webhooks to the new events automatically because some headers ( X-*-Event , X-*-Event-Type ) and the action key have changed, which might break existing receivers. Furthermore, completion notifications are only emitted after all jobs of a run have terminated. !12598

Please inspect existing webhooks and manually migrate them to the workflow run events after verifying that the webhook receivers can process them without issues.

For repositories that contain a FUNDING.yml file, Forgejo shows a new “Donate” button which presents a list of donation options when clicked.

Additionally, for users and organizations that have such file in their .profile repository, a similar button appears on their profile pages.

This feature currently exists only in the web interface, but we are considering to implement an API surface for it. If you have a use cases for such API feature, please help shape it by sharing your feedback in the dedicated issue .

Auto-completion for issues and pull requests

When authoring an issue, pull request, or comment, Forgejo will offer auto-completion for issues and pull requests. !8088 To activate the auto-completion, type # for issues or pull requests, or ! for pull requests only. To refine the suggestions, either continue with a search term or an issue or pull request number.

Forgejo’s Git LFS support is being overhauled. While most changes are under the hood, a string of smaller improvements are visible to users. Those include navigation and overview improvements in the LFS settings, new views to discover the commits that refer to a given LFS file, and better handling of pointers.

Forgejo can be configured so that when adding a user to an organization, they are not added to the organization instantly but instead receive an invitation that can be accepted or declined. This behavior can be enabled by setting [service].ADD_MEMBERS_BY_INVITATIONS = true in Forgejo’s app.ini .

Authentication providers are still able to add users to organizations with no action on their part.

The invitations are visible on the organization profile and are sent out by email. By default they expire after 14 days.

Work is ongoing to make those invitations visible in the in-app notifications.

A user can now be added or invited to multiple teams in one go, without going through each needed team individually. !11848

Markdown contents of comments can now be easily copied via the ellipsis menu. !13083

items.title: Using Artificial Intelligence to reverse engineer hardware
items.content:
After my mother passed away I ended up with a big box full of old film negatives containing photos from childhood family trips and similar. So I decided to buy a negative photo scanner and found that the Plustek 8200i was supported under Linux so I bought that. Only to discover that the chipset in the scanner had changed to one that wasn’t supported under Linux anymore. So I had some success making Linux configuration tools for some of my hardware using Claude code, like my Dell Camera controller app so I thought, maybe Claude can help me get a working SANE driver. I basically got stuck and got nowhere for the longest time and even basically gave up on the project for a few Months.

Then I saw a post on X from Tom Crider aka Glorious Eggroll talking about how he had managed to fix a mouse driver using AI tooling. He basically described how he set it up so that the AI agent had full control of a Windows instance to capture data needed to fix the driver. So I pasted his tweet into Claude and asked it to help me set up a windows virtual machine to do the same things Tom as doing for my scanner. I think the combination of having the ability to run scans under windows and capture the USB data while doing so worked wonders, probably combined with improvements to Claude code made a huge difference. Within a few hours I had my first ever working scan under Linux, sure with some quality issues, but 100% recognizable as the image in the negative. Some days later I had a near perfect driver, including support for Infrared scanning ready to go, only to discover that in the time between me giving up and then trying again someone had committed code to SANE to support the scanner already…..it happens sometimes. I also used Claude to write an application for doing negative scanning, which I named Negative Vibes , thought that was a cute name.

Anyway, with the success of my scanner effort I thought, I wonder if I can use this to finally fix the last issues with MIPI camera support on my laptop. So I told claude to re-use the harness I had created and try to fix the MIPI camera on my laptop by updating the kernel driver and libcamera as needed. I started the job in the morning and by the end of the day I had a much improved situation with patches for both the kernel and libcamera ready.

So I thought that this might be worthwhile sharing with the world, and while anyone could start from scratch I did ask Claude to make the harness generic and document it to make the pathway for anyone else who wants to try this on their hardware a little easier. Writing a driver for undocumented hardware has always been tedious. You capture bus traffic, stare at hex dumps, and form hypotheses about what each register or control transfer does. You then test them one at a time, usually for weeks. None of it is conceptually hard, but it takes a lot of patience and skills.

That kind of work suits an AI model well. It can read thousands of lines of USB capture, notice that a sequence repeats with one byte changing, and propose what that byte means. It can write the test to confirm it, and it doesn’t get bored. The human still decides what to build and checks that it works on real hardware, but the slog shrinks a lot.

Be aware that I did not use hw-harness in this form for my projects as this was basically bespoke code at that time, so this project is an attempt to make the harness more generic and shareable from the scripts I was using while doing the work. What hw-harness is meant to help your Claude or Codex session with:

1. Record a reference session. Run the vendor’s Windows driver in a KVM virtual machine, with the real device passed through to the guest.

2. Capture from outside the VM. Record the traffic on the Linux host with usbmon. It sits below the passthrough layer, so the guest can’t see it.

3. Repeat the same operation on Linux with your own driver, and capture that the same way.

items.title: Miasma Worm Targets AI Coding Agents: 73 Microsoft Azure Repos Disabled
items.content:
An unprecedented supply chain attack bypasses registry-level scanners entirely, turning developer tools including Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI into execution vectors.

The Incident: On June 3, 2026, a highly sophisticated variant of the Miasma worm (also known as Mini Shai-Hulud) launched a coordinated, two-pronged attack targeting both the npm registry and developer source code repositories.

The Escalation: The attack successfully breached multiple high-profile GitHub accounts, including the official Microsoft Azure durabletask repository, using stolen Personal Access Tokens (PATs) and backdated commits to evade traditional audit trails.

The Response: In an ultra-rapid defensive maneuver, GitHub’s automated mitigation systems disabled 73 compromised repositories – including 49 directly associated with Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples within a mere 105-second window .

The Vector: Instead of relying on traditional package installation hooks, Miasma targets the developer’s local environment. It abuses legitimate auto-run, hook, and rule engines within modern IDEs and AI coding assistants ( VS Code, Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI ) to execute a malicious 4.3 MB staged dropper upon folder-open or agent initialization.

The Impact: Once detonated, the Bun-based worm harvests credentials for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, npm, and GitHub, and automatically propagates by committing itself back into any repository the victim’s stolen tokens can write to.

At exactly 16:00 UTC on June 3, 2026, a silent, automated purge swept across GitHub. In a high-speed containment action lasting just 105 seconds, 73 active repositories vanished from the platform. Among them were 49 critical repositories belonging to Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples.

This drastic mitigation followed alarming telemetry indicating that threat actors behind the Miasma malware family had regained write access to key cloud repositories. The compromise exploited a stolen Personal Access Token (PAT) belonging to an active Microsoft contributor.

While security firms like StepSecurity and JFrog scrambled to document an concurrent attack vector on the npm registry where 57 malicious packages were published, a second, far more insidious arm of the campaign was already silently spreading directly inside GitHub source repositories.

By bypassing registries and package managers entirely, the Miasma worm targeted the very tools developers use to write code. It didn’t wait for npm install . Instead, it waited for the developer to simply open their code editor or launch an AI coding assistant.

The genius of the Miasma repository-poisoning campaign lies in its exploit surface. When an attacker successfully pushed malicious commits to targeted codebases (such as the popular library icflorescu/mantine-datatable ), the commits added no actual code dependencies.

Instead, the attacker checked in five innocent-looking workspace configuration files and one obfuscated JavaScript file: .github/setup.js .

│ └── settings . json < - - Claude Code SessionStart Hook

│ └── setup . mdc < - - Cursor Agent Prompt Injection

│ └── settings . json < - - Gemini CLI SessionStart Hook

│ └── tasks . json < - - VS Code Automatic Folder - Open Task

├── package . json < -- Hijacked NPM Test Script

└── setup . js < - - The 4.3 MB Staged Dropper

Each of these configuration files is designed to abuse a legitimate, developer-friendly auto-run feature within popular modern tools. Opening the cloned directory in any of these environments instantly triggers execution.

Claude Code & Gemini CLI (SessionStart Hooks)

Both Anthropic’s Claude Code and Google’s Gemini CLI support custom hooks triggered when an AI agent initializes a session in a project workspace. Miasma exploits this by defining a blanket wildcard matcher that forces the agent to execute the dropper via Node.js before any developer prompt is processed.

items.title: My self-hosted infrastructure with Incus OS
items.summary: devops, linux
items.content:
For the last seven months, I spent a good part of my (small amount of) free time rebuilding my self-hosting infrastructure at home. I wanted something secure, fully automated, that updates itself and that I can rebuild from scratch if something goes wrong. Most of the ideas come from my work on infrastructures following SecNumCloud (a French security standard for cloud providers) and, to a lesser extent, ISO 27001, I wanted to see how far I could apply the same principles at home.

In this blog post, I will explain how my personal infrastructure works, how all the pieces fit together, and why I think each security layer is useful. This is not a step by step guide, I will not go deep into code, the goal is to show the architecture and the reasons behind it.

Before going further, I need to be honest, this is a personal infrastructure running on a single machine at home, and it is probably totally overengineered for most people. If you just want to host a Nextcloud for your family, a lot of what follows is not needed. But I learned a lot along the way, especially about containers and cloud-init, and I am very happy with the result :)

The hosting server is nothing special, just a regular laptop with 16 GB of RAM, a NVMe SSD and a network card, sitting next to my Internet provider box.

Everything runs on this laptop. The operating system is Incus OS, a small immutable system that only run Incus, a manager for system containers and virtual machines (it is like Proxmox but more container oriented).

On top of it, there are about twenty Ubuntu system containers, one per service, and two virtual machines for the more sensitive parts. Inside each system container, the applications themselves run as podman containers, described with "quadlets", which are files that systemd turns into services. So there are two levels of containers: Incus instances, and podman containers inside them.

I am currently hosting the following services:

Immich for photos/videos dumped from smartphones

Uptime Kuma and SmokePing to monitor the network

a monitoring stack: Prometheus, Grafana, Loki, Alertmanager

Nothing is configured by hand. Everything is declared from a git repository with OpenTofu (the open source fork of Terraform) and cloud-init (the tool that configures a cloud system at its first boot).

The system containers are unprivileged, which means the root user inside a container is not root on the host. Compared to a VM per service, this is very efficient: the RAM and disk usage are much lower, and everything is pretty fast.

Here is a diagram of how everything fits together:

Incus OS is the foundation, I chose it because it is locked as much as possible. It comes with:

A/B boot: the update is written on the other partition, and the system can go back to the previous one if needed

no local access: there is no shell, no SSH, no package manager, nothing can be done with local access to the laptop

disk encryption with the TPM (this allows auto reboot without typing a passphrase, but if someone steals the laptop it will boot and they would be able to attack the system locally as if they were on my LAN)

It is not exposed on the Internet, I manage it from my LAN through the Incus API using a certificate for authentication.

An unexepcted side effect is that I do not use SSH anymore to manage the infrastructure. No SSH keys to manage, no SSH endpoint to secure, no TERM variable issue. When I need to look inside an instance, I can use incus exec to run a command or incus shell to open a shell, all through the Incus API. The only SSH in the whole setup is the git over SSH access provided by Forgejo, which is an application feature.

This is probably the part I like the most. Each instance is created from a fresh Ubuntu cloud image, and cloud-init does everything at first boot: upgrade the system, install podman, write the quadlet files, decrypt the secrets, start the services. I took inspiration from my experience with Qubes OS.

I’m writing this because I recently found out about a silent and incredibly anti-consumer change Withings just implemented, and I think the whole community needs to be aware of it.

Starting from October 13th, 2026, any new Withings account is forced to pay for a Withings+ subscription ($99.99/year) just to sync their own data to Apple Health.

I reached out to Customer Support and their response was completely contradictory. They claimed that syncing with Apple Health is a "standard feature that does not require a subscription," but in the very next sentence, they confirmed that "any account created after October 13th will be asked to sign up for a Withings+ subscription in order to export data" justifying it with new "privacy measures" and an "AI connector".

Let's be clear: writing data to Apple Health via HealthKit happens locally on the phone. It does not require complex cloud compute, server costs, or any "AI connector". It's a basic API call. I know we can still manually export a CSV file, but let's be real—nobody wants to manually import CSV files in 2026. Even the absolute cheapest, no-name smart scales on the market offer automatic Apple Health synchronization for free.

Taking a fundamental feature that has always been free and locking it behind a paywall for new users is an obvious cash grab. It ruins the hardware experience and destroys the trust in the brand.

items.title: Zero-day exploit completely defeats default Windows 11 BitLocker protections
items.content:
A zero-day exploit circulating online allows people with physical access to a Windows 11 system to bypass default BitLocker protections and gain complete access to an encrypted drive within seconds.

The exploit, named YellowKey, was published earlier this week by a researcher who goes by the alias Nightmare-Eclipse. It reliably bypasses default Windows 11 deployments of BitLocker, the full-volume encryption protection Microsoft provides to make disk contents off-limits to anyone without the decryption key, which is stored in a secured piece of hardware known as a trusted platform module (TPM). BitLocker is a mandatory protection for many organizations, including those that contract with governments.

When one disk volume manipulates another

The core of the YellowKey exploit is a custom-made FsTx folder. Online documentation of this folder is hard to find. As explained later, the directory associated with the file fstx.dll appears to involve what Microsoft calls the transactional NTFS , which allows developers to have “transactional atomicity” for file operations in transactions with a single file, multiple files, or ones that span multiple sources.

The steps for carrying out the bypass are simple:

Copy the custom FsTx folder from the Nightmare-Eclipse exploit page to an NTFS- or FAT-formatted USB drive

Connect the USB drive to the BitLocker-protected device

Boot up the device and immediately press and hold down the [Ctrl] key

There are at least two ways to accomplish the third step. One way is to boot into Windows, hold down the [Shift] key, click on the power icon, and click restart. Another is to power on the device and restart it as soon as Windows starts booting.

In either case, a command (CMD.EXE) prompt appears. The prompt has full access to the entire drive contents, allowing an attacker to copy, modify, or delete them. In a normal Windows Recovery flow, the attacker would need to enter a BitLocker recovery key. Somehow, the YellowKey exploit bypasses this safeguard. Multiple researchers, including Kevin Beaumont and Will Dormann , have confirmed the exploit works as described here.

It’s unclear what in the custom FsTx folder causes the bypass. Dormann said that it appears to be related to Transactional NTFS, which itself uses command-log file system under the hood. Dormann further noted that by looking at the Windows fstx.dll, one will see code that explicitly looks for \System Volume Information\FsTx in the FsTxFindSessions() function.”

The contents of this FsTx directory used in the YellowKey exploit reveal no strings related to RecoverySimulation.ini. It does, however, show the files and paths \??\C:\Windows\win.ini and

\??\X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini, “where X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini is what controls what WinRE [Windows Recovery] does when it fires up.”

Dormann, who is a senior principal vulnerability analyst at Tharros Labs, continued:

But what’s intriguing to me is: Why can the presence a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume affect the contents of ANOTHER VOLUME when it’s replayed? 🤔

In a normal WinRE session, you have a X:\Windows\System32 directory that has a winpeshl.ini file in it:

However, with the YellowKey exploit, it looks like Transactional NTFS bits on a USB Drive are able to delete the winpeshl.ini file on ANOTHER DRIVE (X:). And we get a cmd.exe prompt, with bitlocker unlocked instead of the expected Windows Recovery environment. While the TPM-only Bitlocker bypass is indeed interesting, I think the buried lede here is that a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume has the ability to modify the contents of another volume when it is replayed. To me, this in and of itself sounds like a vulnerability.

A Microsoft representative declined to answer questions sent by email about the reported vulnerability other than to say the company is investigating.

Meta releases Muse Spark Open, a new ‘open-weight’ AI model

Meta says Muse excels at ‘multi-step reasoning’ and ‘complex software engineering’ as it races to catch up to Chinese rivals

Meta on Thursday launched a new open-weight AI model which it claims rivals, and in some cases outperforms, similar products from leading Chinese developers.

Muse Spark Open “is the most capable US open-weight model to date,” Meta’s chief of AI Alexandr Wang wrote on X.

Unlike so-called closed models – such as Anthropic’s Claude or OpenAI’s ChatGPT – developers can download the parameters, known as weights and biases, of an open-weight model and modify them.

‘Charming and disarming’ … how Meta’s technology-packed Muse harnesses the power of cuteness

Chinese developers have emerged as dominant players in the open-weight market for AI models over the past couple of years.

Alibaba’s Qwen, Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 and Z.ai’s GLM models have been considered open-weight frontrunners globally, but Meta claims its new open model now competes on a similar level.

“Built for coding and agentic work,” Muse Spark Open “excels at long-horizon tasks, complex software engineering, and multi-step reasoning,” Meta said in a blogpost, adding that “strong safeguards” have been integrated into the new model.

Muse Spark Open is also “optimized” to run on Apple’s advanced M5 Ultra chips, Meta said, signaling an unusual partnership between the two tech companies.

Muse Spark Open requires significant computing power. Users can run the model on two Mac Studios with M5 Ultra chips to create a “supercomputer” on their own desktop, Meta said.

The launch comes just days after Meta announced its newest closed model, which it said rivalled the most advanced versions of ChatGPT and Claude.

Meta’s AI efforts were initially focused on open models, but more recently Zuckerberg has pushed the company to compete with OpenAI and Anthropic.

items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-93681 📢 Source: Wordfence 💣 CVSS Score: 0.0 (NA) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: False The Tutor LMS – eLearning and online course solution plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Stored Cross-Site Scripting via display_name Parameter in all versions up to, and including, 4.1.0 due to insufficient input sanitization and output escaping. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with subscriber-level access and above, to inject arbitrary web scripts in pages that will execute whenever a user accesses an injected page.
